title: pH of a Weak Acid
short: Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for [H₃O⁺], then take the pH.
trouble: Students treat a weak acid as fully ionized, setting [H₃O⁺] equal to the acid's concentration.

blocks.html: For a weak acid, $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$ is not the acid's concentration; only a small part ionizes. Its Ka and an ICE table give the answer, and the small-x approximation usually makes it quick.
For a weak acid at concentration $C$: $K_a = \dfrac{x^2}{C - x}$ with $x = [\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$. If $x$ is under 5% of $C$, then $x \approx \sqrt{K_aC}$. Then $\text{pH} = -\log x$.

Each HA that ionizes makes one $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$ and one $\mathrm{A^-}$, so both equal $x$, and $C - x$ acid is left. The water's own $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$ ($10^{-7}\ \text{M}$ at most) is tiny next to $x$ in any ordinary weak acid solution, so it is ignored. Because $K_a$ is small, $x$ is usually much smaller than $C$, which lets you drop it from $C - x$.

blocks.name: ch-particles
blocks.cap: Same concentration, different strength: HCl is fully ionized, while only a small fraction of acetic acid molecules give up their protons at any moment.

blocks.title: Acetic acid
blocks.q: Find the pH of $0.10\ \text{M}$ acetic acid, $K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$.

blocks.title: Ka from a measured pH
blocks.q: A $0.050\ \text{M}$ solution of a weak acid has pH 3.00. Find $K_a$.

blocks.html: Two assumptions hide inside the shortcut, and both can be checked. The 5% test checks that $x$ is small next to $C$. And we ignored the $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$ that water itself provides; that is safe as long as $x$ is much larger than $10^{-7}\ \text{M}$, which is true unless the acid is extremely weak or extremely dilute. The percent ionization lesson shows what happens as an acid is diluted.

Treating a weak acid as fully ionized, so that $0.10\ \text{M}$ acetic acid would have pH 1.00. A weak acid gives far less $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$ than its concentration. Check: a weak acid's pH must be higher than that of a strong acid at the same concentration.
